title: What If the Cosmos Evolves Like a Living Organism?
summary:
Evolution explains how peacocks got their dazzling tails and why chimps resemble humans. But could the same Darwinian principles apply to the entire universe? A small but growing group of thinkers says yes. They call it 'cosmological evolution,' and it's one of the most mind-bending ideas in modern physics.

The concept traces back to physicist Lee Smolin, who in 1992 proposed that black holes might spawn new universes. According to this theory, when matter collapses into a singularity inside a black hole, it could rebound and expand into a new cosmos with slightly different physical laws. If those new universes inherit traits from their parent universes—just as organisms inherit genes—then universes could evolve through a form of cosmic natural selection. Universes that produce more black holes would have more offspring, so over countless generations, most universes would be optimized for black hole production. Smolin argued that our universe, with its abundance of black holes, fits that prediction.

For decades, Smolin's idea sat on the fringes of theoretical physics. But recently, it's found an unexpected champion: Julian Gough, an Irish writer best known for penning the ending of the video game Minecraft. Gough stumbled upon Smolin's work while pondering why the universe has become more complex over time—from a hot ball of gas to stars, planets, and life. 'It seemed to me an evolutionary explanation was the natural one,' Gough says. He now writes about the theory on his Substack blog, The Egg and the Rock, and has connected it to puzzling observations from the James Webb Space Telescope, which has spotted surprisingly mature galaxies in the early universe.

Gough admits he's not a physicist, but he argues that Smolin's theory 'hasn't been falsified. It just hasn't been engaged with properly at all.' Some futurist philosophers have extended the idea, suggesting that technologically advanced civilizations might eventually create artificial black holes, thereby increasing their universe's reproductive success.

Of course, cosmological evolution remains highly speculative. There's no direct evidence that black holes create universes, and many physicists remain skeptical. But the idea is provocative. If true, it would mean the cosmos is not a static rock but a living, evolving entity—an egg that keeps hatching new realities. As Gough puts it, 'The universe is not a rock. It is an egg.'
why_it_matters: This idea matters because it stretches the boundary between biology and physics, inviting us to ask whether the laws of nature themselves could change over time. If even partly true, it would reframe the universe as a living, evolving system with a history and family tree—not a fixed stage on which events happen.

background_read: Charles Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection is usually applied to living organisms: traits that help an organism survive and reproduce become more common over generations.

Lee Smolin (an American theoretical physicist) extended that logic beyond biology in 1992, proposing that black holes might collapse and rebound into new universes with slightly altered physical laws.

Julian Gough (an Irish writer who helped write the ending of the video game Minecraft) has become an unusual champion of Smolin's idea, arguing that an evolutionary explanation fits why the cosmos grew more complex.

The James Webb Space Telescope (the most powerful space telescope ever launched, operated by NASA and international partners) has spotted surprisingly mature galaxies in the early universe, which some think fits Smolin's framework.

Mainstream physics treats the idea as speculative because no direct evidence currently shows that black holes create universes, and many scientists prefer explanations that can be tested more directly.

perspectives.description: For champions like Lee Smolin and Julian Gough, cosmological evolution offers a natural explanation for why our universe seems tuned to produce black holes. It also links the most powerful idea in biology—natural selection—to the history of the entire cosmos.

Many physicists remain skeptical because the theory currently lacks direct evidence. An untestable or unfalsified idea can be intellectually appealing, but it may not meet the strict standards required for a scientific claim.

The debate echoes a pattern in science: bold ideas can sit on the fringe for decades, then gain attention when new observations, such as surprisingly mature early galaxies, force researchers to re-examine old assumptions.

The next step is to look for observable signatures that could distinguish universe-spawning black holes from ordinary ones. If such tests become possible, cosmological evolution could move from speculation toward a testable scientific program.
